name: Bias in a sampling distribution
quote: In the context of sampling distributions, bias means that the sampling distribution of an estimator is not centered on the population parameter.
plain_en: estimator distribution not centered on parameter

name: Unbiased estimator
quote: An estimator is unbiased if, on average, it does not underestimate or overestimate the population parameter.
plain_en: estimator averages to the population parameter

name: Point estimator
quote: Sample statistics are point estimators for population parameters.
plain_en: sample statistic used to estimate a parameter

name: Sampling distribution of a sample proportion
quote: The set of all sample proportions is approximately normally distributed.
plain_en: distribution of sample proportions from repeated samples

name: Mean of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion
quote: The mean of the set of sample proportions equals p, the population proportion.
plain_en: sample proportion averages to population proportion

name: Standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion
quote: The standard deviation of the set of sample proportions is approximately equal to
plain_en: spread of sample proportions decreases with n

name: Randomization condition
quote: The randomization condition: The data should be collected using a random sample.
plain_en: data come from a random sample

name: 10% condition
quote: The 10% condition: When sampling without replacement, the sample size n should be no larger than 10% of the population.
plain_en: sample no more than ten percent of population

name: Normality condition for proportions
quote: The normality condition: The number of successes, np, and the number of failures, n(1 − p), should both be at least 10.
plain_en: at least ten successes and ten failures

name: Confidence interval
quote: First, there is the confidence interval. This gives an interval of plausible values and is expressed in the following form: estimate ± margin of error
plain_en: range of plausible parameter values

name: Confidence level
quote: Second, there is the success rate for the method, called the confidence level. This is the proportion of times repeated applications of this method would capture the true population parameter.
plain_en: long-run success rate of the method

name: Critical value z*
quote: where the critical value, z*, depends on the chosen confidence level.
plain_en: multiplier set by the confidence level

name: One-sample z-interval for a population proportion
quote: Naming the procedure is most easily done by simply stating “one-sample z-interval for a population proportion.”
plain_en: confidence interval for one proportion

name: Interpreting a confidence level
quote: Second, we can interpret the confidence level and say that if this survey were conducted many times, about 90% of the resulting confidence intervals would contain the true proportion of voters who favor the bond issue.
plain_en: percent of intervals capturing the parameter

name: Choosing sample size for a proportion
quote: A formula for choosing the sample size n for a specific margin of error, MOE, can be found by algebraically solving for n in the equation to obtain:
plain_en: sample size needed for a margin of error

name: Null hypothesis
quote: The general testing procedure is to choose a specific hypothesis to be tested, called the null hypothesis, pick an appropriate random sample, and then use measurements from the sample to determine the likelihood of the null hypothesis.
plain_en: hypothesis of no effect or no difference

name: Alternative hypothesis
quote: There is an alternative hypothesis, stated in the form of a strict inequality (for example, Ha: p < 0.37 or Ha: p > 0.37 or Ha: p ≠ 0.37).
plain_en: hypothesis the test hopes to support

name: p-value
quote: The strength of the sample statistic can be gauged through its associated p-value, which is the probability of obtaining a sample statistic as extreme (or more extreme) as the one obtained if the null hypothesis is assumed to be true.
plain_en: probability of results as extreme under null

name: Significance level
quote: The significance level, α, is fixed at the beginning of the hypothesis test.
plain_en: threshold fixed before the test

name: Type I error
quote: The α-risk, also called the significance level of the test, is the probability of committing a Type I error and mistakenly rejecting a true null hypothesis.
plain_en: rejecting a true null hypothesis

name: Type II error
quote: A Type II error, a mistaken failure to reject a false null hypothesis, has associated probability β.
plain_en: failing to reject a false null hypothesis

name: Power
quote: The power of a hypothesis test is the probability that a Type II error is not committed. That is, given a true alternative, the power is the probability of rejecting the false null hypothesis.
plain_en: probability of rejecting a false null

name: One-sided test
quote: For a one-sided test (the alternative is < or >), the p-value is the proportion of values at or more extreme than the test statistic (in the direction of the alternative).
plain_en: test with a directional alternative

name: Two-sided test
quote: For a two-sided test (the alternative is ≠), the p-value is the proportion of values at or more extreme than the test statistic in either direction; that is, it is twice the calculated tail probability.
plain_en: test with a not-equal alternative

name: Decision rule for a hypothesis test
quote: If the p-value ≤α, reject H0; there is convincing evidence for Ha. If the p-value >α, fail to reject H0; there is not convincing evidence for Ha.
plain_en: compare p-value with significance level

name: One-sample z-test for a population proportion
quote: Procedure: One-sample z-test for a population proportion.
plain_en: hypothesis test for one proportion

name: Sampling distribution of the difference in sample proportions
quote: The set of all differences of sample proportions is approximately normally distributed.
plain_en: distribution of differences between sample proportions

name: Mean of the difference in sample proportions
quote: The mean of the set of differences of sample proportions equals p1 − p2, the difference of population proportions.
plain_en: difference averages to population difference

name: Standard deviation of the difference in sample proportions
quote: The standard deviation of the set of differences of sample proportions is approximately equal to
plain_en: spread of difference between sample proportions

name: Randomization condition for two samples
quote: The randomization condition: The data should be collected using random samples, and the samples must be taken independently of each other.
plain_en: independent random samples required

name: Normality condition for two proportions
quote: The normality condition: The numbers of successes, n1 p1 and n2 p2, and the numbers of failures, n1(1 − p1) and n2(1 − p2), should all be at least 10.
plain_en: at least ten successes and failures per group

name: Two-sample z-interval for a difference in proportions
quote: A confidence interval for the difference of two proportions will take the following form:
plain_en: interval estimate for difference of proportions

name: Null hypothesis for a difference of two proportions
quote: The null hypothesis for a difference of two proportions is H0 : p1 = p2.
plain_en: hypothesis that two proportions are equal

name: Alternative hypothesis for a difference of two proportions
quote: The alternative hypothesis is Ha : p1 > p2, Ha : p1 < p2, or Ha : p1 ≠ p2.
plain_en: hypothesis that proportions differ

name: Pooled proportion
quote: With a null hypothesis of H0 : p1 = p2, we use the combined (or pooled) proportion in the normality condition and in calculating the standard error.
plain_en: combined proportion used under equal proportions

name: Two-sample z-test for a difference in proportions
quote: Procedure: Two-sample z-test for a difference of two population proportions.
plain_en: hypothesis test comparing two proportions

name: Chi-square test for independence
quote: We cross-classify a single sample of observations from a single population in two ways and then ask whether the two variables are independent of each other. This leads to chi-square tests for independence with hypotheses:
plain_en: test association between two categorical variables

name: Chi-square test for homogeneity
quote: There is a related class of problems in which we have a single categorical variable and obtain independent samples from two or more populations to determine whether the distributions of that variable are different for the populations. This leads to chi-square tests for homogeneity with hypotheses:
plain_en: test whether distributions differ across populations

name: Expected values condition
quote: The expected values condition: All expected values should be greater than 5.
plain_en: all expected cell counts exceed five

name: Expected values
quote: Expected values are calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true.
plain_en: cell counts expected under the null

name: Chi-square statistic
quote: The significance of the differences is gauged by a χ2-value of weighted squared differences defined by:
plain_en: weighted sum of squared differences

name: Degrees of freedom for a chi-square test
quote: df = (rows – 1)(columns – 1)
plain_en: rows minus one times columns minus one

name: Chi-square distribution
quote: the χ2-distribution is a continuous distribution. Applying it to counting data is just an approximation.
plain_en: continuous approximation for count data

name: Margin of error
quote: The percent is the percent of samples that would pinpoint the unknown p within plus or minus respective margins of error.
plain_en: half-width of a confidence interval
